opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What stood out most was how clearly it frames formal theorem proving as more than a niche corner of AI. It argues that it may be one of the cleanest testbeds we have for real reasoning.

The core point is verification. In most domains where we train language models, it's hard to know whether an answer is actually right. You rely on human preference, on benchmarks that leak into training data, or on heuristics. In a formal system like Lean, a proof either type-checks or it doesn't. That gives you a perfectly reliable reward signal. So you can do reinforcement learning, search, and self-play without worrying that the model is just learning to sound convincing. For someone like me who came from mathematics, that was striking. The thing mathematicians care about most, rigor, is exactly what makes the problem tractable for machines.

The second thing was its honesty about the bottlenecks. Data scarcity is a real issue. There's vastly more informal math, in textbooks, papers, and forum posts, than there is formalized math in libraries like Mathlib. So autoformalization, translating natural-language math into formal statements and proofs, becomes a central problem. It's also a hard one, because a statement can be formalized in a way that's subtly wrong, and then you've proven the wrong thing perfectly.

Third, I liked that it looked beyond competition problems. Olympiad-style results get the headlines, and they matter, but the bigger vision is research-level mathematics and, beyond that, verified software and hardware. If you can generate code together with a machine-checkable proof that it meets its specification, the implications for safety and reliability are enormous.

So my overall takeaway was that formal theorem proving sits at an intersection. It needs good intuition, which is what language models are getting better at, and it needs rigor, which is what proof assistants guarantee. Bringing those two together feels like one of the most exciting things happening right now, and it's a big part of why I chose to work in this space.

r001.rationale: The response says formal theorem proving combines intuition and rigor, but it does not identify the survey’s question about the capabilities of a good AI mathematician as something that stood out.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me first was actually the framing in the title, because I think it gets the direction right but maybe for a reason the paper only partly spells out. People sometimes treat formal proving as a niche, almost a curiosity for a few mathematicians who like Lean. But if you read the survey as a story about verification rather than about mathematics, it becomes much bigger. Formal proof is one of the only domains where a model can generate something open-ended and creative, and then get a signal that is completely trustworthy. Not a human rater, not a majority vote, not another model saying "looks good to me." A kernel checks it, and it is either right or it is not. That is a very rare property, and the survey does a nice job of showing how much of the recent progress is really downstream of that one fact.

The second thing I appreciated is how honestly it lays out the bottlenecks. There is a tendency in this field to celebrate benchmark numbers, and the survey does cover the trajectory from early tree search systems through the competition-level results. But the parts I kept coming back to were the sections on autoformalization and on data. The amount of formalized mathematics in the world is tiny compared to the informal literature. Mathlib is a huge community achievement, and it is still a small fraction of what a working mathematician knows. So the real question is not "can a model close a goal state," it is "can a model take a messy human statement, turn it into a correct formal statement, and then prove it." Getting the statement wrong is a silent failure. You can prove something perfectly and have proven the wrong theorem. I think the paper is right to treat that as a first-class problem rather than a preprocessing step.

The third thing, and this is where I probably read it with my own bias, is the gap between competition problems and research mathematics. Olympiad problems are wonderful because they are self-contained and have clean answers. But research math is about building definitions, choosing the right abstraction, managing a proof that is hundreds of lemmas long, and knowing which direction is even worth exploring. The survey gestures at this transition, at things like long-horizon planning, library-scale reasoning, and the interaction between informal intuition and formal rigor. I would have liked even more there, because I think that is the frontier the title is really pointing at. The competition results are the proof of concept. The interesting part is whether these systems can start contributing to mathematics that no human has written down yet, and do it in a way where we never have to take their word for it.

astra-6.text: I haven’t read it closely enough to give you a fair assessment of the survey itself. But the question its title raises is fascinating: can AI produce a mathematical argument that can actually be checked, rather than one that just sounds convincing? There’s also a distinction between finding a proof and verifying it. A verifier can tell you whether your steps are valid; finding the right definitions, intermediate results, and overall strategy is a different challenge. That’s the part I’d be most interested in seeing the survey unpack.

sol-6.1.text:
What stood out to me was the framing of formal theorem proving as a meeting point between mathematical reasoning and machine learning. A proof assistant gives you a precise way to check whether an argument is valid, but finding that argument still requires creativity: choosing the right intermediate statements, drawing on existing results, and deciding which direction to pursue.

That makes it an interesting frontier for AI. Verification gives you a clear signal of correctness, but it doesn’t automatically make discovery easy. The challenge is turning that reliable feedback into systems that can find useful proofs—and eventually help mathematicians explore new ideas.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the challenge of AI discovering proofs, but does not identify the survey’s question about what capabilities a good AI mathematician should possess as something that stood out.
